summary: Discusses how three major bibliographic identifiers, ISBN, ISSN and SICI, can be used within the Uniform Resource Name framework. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Books and magazines already have ID numbers. This explains how to use those numbers as permanent names on the Internet.

questions: how to use isbn as a urn
subtitle: A feasibility study showing that ISBN, ISSN and SICI library identifiers fit inside the URN syntax.

tldr.problem: The URN framework needed proof that it could carry identifiers from existing, widely used naming systems, such as those used by libraries and publishers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo shows how the ISBN, ISSN and SICI can be written as URNs (for example URN:ISBN:0-395-36341-1), with extra comparison rules and %-encoding where needed.
tldr.outcome: It demonstrates feasibility only. It does not define an official standard, and any real one would need the responsible standards bodies.

facts.label: ISBN length
facts.value: Ten digits, last may be X

today: RFC 2288 is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a feasibility demonstration, not a standard for encoding these identifiers.

sections.title: Purpose and Caveats
sections.content:
The URN working group wanted to show that the URN syntax (RFC 2141) can accommodate identifiers from established namespaces. This memo picks the bibliographic community and three identifiers: the ISBN for books, the ISSN for serials as a whole, and the SICI for individual issues or articles.

The authors are explicit that this only demonstrates feasibility. It was not developed with the bodies that maintain these identifiers, and any actual standard would have to be. The namespace identifiers (NIDs) ISBN, ISSN and SICI are used for illustration; the memo notes alternatives, such as one single bibliographic namespace.
sections.eli5: Before building a big system, you test it with a few real examples. This memo is that test, using book and magazine numbers.

sections.title: Identification Versus Resolution
sections.content:
A URN names a thing; resolving it is a separate step. The ISSN 0040-781X identifies the magazine "Time" as a whole, every issue ever published, so resolving it should not dump hundreds of thousands of pages on the user. A navigational system such as a search form is more reasonable.

ISBNs and SICIs identify finite objects, but even those may be large enough that a hierarchical resolution is appropriate. The thing named may also exist only in print, in which case the best a resolver can offer is information on where to get it, such as library holdings or a publisher order form.
sections.eli5: A name tells you which book you mean. Finding the book is a different job, and sometimes the answer is just "it is on this library shelf".

sections.title: ISBN: Books
sections.content:
An ISBN identifies an edition of a monographic work. It is a ten-digit number whose last digit can also be the letter X, split into a group identifier, a publisher identifier, a title identifier and a modulus 11 check digit.

All ISBN characters are valid in a URN, so %-encoding is never needed. The example is URN:ISBN:0-395-36341-1. Before comparing two ISBN URNs, hyphens should be removed and any X converted to upper case.

Practice varies on when a new ISBN is assigned, for example for paperback versus hardback, and the URN simply reflects that. An ISBN URN will often resolve to many instances of the work.
sections.eli5: An ISBN is a book's own number. When comparing two, ignore the dashes and use a capital X, so that two ways of writing the same number match.

sections.title: ISSN: Serials
sections.content:
An ISSN identifies a work published continuously in issues, such as a journal or newspaper, as a whole. It has the form NNNN-NNNN, where the last character may be an upper case X from the check character calculation. Blocks of numbers are handed to regional centers and publishers, so the ISSN has little internal structure.

As with ISBNs, no %-encoding is needed, and hyphens should be dropped and x normalized to upper case before comparison. The example is URN:ISSN:1046-8188.

Bibliographic practice varies, for instance for annual conference proceedings, which are treated as serials by some and as monographs with ISBNs by others. Name changes and print versus electronic editions also affect when new ISSNs are assigned. The URN inherits these judgments.
sections.eli5: An ISSN is the number for a whole magazine, not one copy of it. Like ISBNs, you compare them after dropping the dash.

sections.title: SICI: Issues and Articles
sections.content:
A SICI identifies a serial issue or a contribution within an issue, such as an article or a table of contents. It is defined by NISO/ANSI Z39.56-1997. Unlike an ISBN or ISSN it is not assigned but constructed from information about the item. It begins with the ISSN, followed by chronology in parentheses and enumeration (volume and number), then a contribution segment such as <62:KTSW> (starting page and title code), and a control segment with a check character.

The SICI character set includes characters that are reserved or excluded in URN syntax, and these must be %-encoded. The memo's examples are URN:SICI:1046-8188(199501)13:1%3C%3E1.0.TX;2-F for an issue and URN:SICI:1046-8188(199501)13:1%3C69:FTTHBI%3E2.0.TX;2-4 for an article.

The memo proposes no lexical equivalence rules for SICIs, leaving that to resolvers. Because a SICI can be built from varying information, several codes may represent the same article.
sections.eli5: A SICI is like a precise address for one article: the magazine, the date, the issue and the page. Some special characters have to be written in a coded way so they fit in a URN.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo covers only how to encode the identifiers. Resolution is not discussed, so secure or authenticated resolution is out of scope. It also does not address validating the integrity or source of URNs containing bibliographic identifiers, nor intellectual property rights in the identified objects or in databases used to build resolvers.
sections.eli5: This memo only shows how to write the names. It does not say how to keep them safe or who owns the books.

references.text: Sollins, K., and L. Masinter, "Functional Requirements for Uniform Resource Names", RFC 1737, December 1994.
